# Technical Brief: Optimizing Compiler Internals

## 1. SSA Construction

**Cytron et al. dominance-frontier algorithm.** Builds a dominator tree, computes each node's dominance frontier (the set of nodes where a definition's influence stops dominating but still reaches via some control path), then places φ-nodes at iterated dominance frontiers (DF⁺) of every definition site. Guarantees minimal SSA (no redundant φ-nodes) but requires full dominator-tree computation (Lengauer-Tarjan, O(E·log V) or near-linear) before any φ-node insertion, making it better suited to AOT optimizing compilers (GCC, LLVM's `-O2`+ paths) where upfront analysis cost is amortized.

**Braun et al. simple/local-first construction.** Builds SSA incrementally during a single pass over the CFG without precomputing dominance frontiers. Each basic block tracks local variable definitions; reads of a variable not locally defined trigger `readVariableRecursive`, which recurses into predecessors. Blocks with unresolved predecessors (loop headers before back edges are known) are marked unsealed and get an operandless φ placeholder; once all predecessors are known the block is "sealed" and the φ operands are filled in. Trivial φ-nodes (all operands identical or self-referential) are removed via `tryRemoveTrivialPhi`, yielding pruned, minimal SSA without ever computing dominance frontiers explicitly. This locality makes it the preferred method for JIT/one-pass compilers (Cranelift, early-stage LLVM lowering, V8's Turbofan-style graph builders) where single-pass construction cost matters more than asymptotic elegance.

**Sreedhar & Gao DJ-graph algorithm.** Augments the dominator tree with "join edges" (D-edges from the dominator tree plus J-edges for actual CFG edges that aren't tree edges) to compute iterated dominance frontiers in close to linear time, avoiding the worst-case quadratic behavior of naively iterating Cytron's DF computation on pathological CFGs. Used when an implementation needs the Cytron-style guarantees but at better asymptotic cost for large functions.

**SSA destruction / out-of-SSA translation.** Converting back to non-SSA form for code generation requires replacing φ-nodes with explicit copies at predecessor block ends. Naive copy insertion can hit the **lost-copy problem** (a value is overwritten before a parallel copy that should have preserved it executes) and the **swap problem** (two values need to be exchanged, which a sequence of plain moves cannot do without a temporary). The standard fix is to treat all φ-related copies at a predecessor as a **parallel copy** and sequentialize them correctly (introducing a temporary register for cycles), as formalized by Sreedhar et al.'s and later Boissinot et al.'s algorithms. **Coalescing** during destruction merges SSA values that end up in the same non-SSA variable to avoid redundant copies, directly feeding into register allocation's own coalescing phase.

**Static Single Information (SSI) form.** Extends SSA by adding σ-functions at branch points (splitting a value's live range per successor) in addition to φ-functions at merge points, giving every *use* site, not just every definition, a unique name. This benefits sparse conditional constant propagation and range analysis but at higher node-count cost, so it's used selectively rather than as a default IR.

**Trade-offs.** Braun's method is near-optimal for single-pass/JIT pipelines; Cytron/Sreedhar-Gao remain standard in AOT compilers that already compute dominator trees for other analyses (post-dominance, loop detection) and want the minimality guarantee without re-deriving it heuristically.

## 2. Alias Analysis

**Andersen's analysis.** Inclusion-based (subset) points-to analysis: each assignment `p = q` generates a constraint `pts(q) ⊆ pts(p)`, solved to fixpoint over points-to sets. Flow-insensitive and (typically) context-insensitive in its base form, with worst-case cubic time in program size (because points-to sets can grow and constraints must be re-propagated). Precise relative to unification-based approaches because it does not merge points-to sets of unified variables, only propagates subsets.

**Steensgaard's analysis.** Unification-based: variables that may alias are unioned into equivalence classes via union-find, giving near-linear time (O(n log n)-ish in practice) at a real precision cost, since once two variables are unified their entire points-to sets merge permanently, overapproximating aliasing more aggressively than Andersen's. Used where scalability on very large codebases matters more than precision (e.g. early-stage whole-program analyses).

**Type-Based Alias Analysis (TBAA).** Uses the source language's type system (and, in C/C++, the strict aliasing rule) to assume that accesses through incompatible pointer types cannot alias, barring explicit `char*`/aggregate exceptions. LLVM encodes this as `!tbaa` metadata attached to memory operations, derived from a type hierarchy DAG; two accesses may-alias only if their TBAA nodes share an ancestor relationship. Cheap to query (near O(1) per pair) but unsound if the source program violates strict aliasing (requiring `-fno-strict-aliasing` to disable).

**Flow-sensitivity and context-sensitivity.** Flow-insensitive analyses (Andersen's, Steensgaard's base forms) compute one points-to set per variable valid at all program points, trading precision for speed. Flow-sensitive variants recompute points-to information per program point, essential for stack/heap reasoning and for precision after strong updates. Context-sensitivity (k-CFA style for higher-order/indirect calls, or the call-string approach cloning summaries per call-site chain up to depth k) avoids merging callee effects across unrelated call sites, at cost exponential in k without memoization.

**MOD/REF summaries and must-alias vs may-alias.** Downstream passes rarely query raw points-to sets directly; instead, alias analysis exposes a may-alias/must-alias oracle plus MOD (modifies) and REF (references) side-effect summaries per call or memory operation. GVN (global value numbering) uses may-alias to decide whether a load can be forwarded from a prior store; LICM uses MOD summaries to determine whether a loop body may write a location before hoisting a load out of the loop. Must-alias (provably identical memory location) enables strong updates and redundant-store elimination; may-alias (possibly the same location) is conservative and used to block unsafe reordering.

*(Full depth versions of these two sections, and sections 3–6, were produced independently by three specialist sub-analyses; the above reflects the consolidated, verified content from that work.)*

## 3. Register Allocation

**Chaitin-Briggs graph coloring.** Build an interference graph where nodes are live ranges/virtual registers and edges connect ranges live simultaneously. Repeatedly simplify by pushing nodes with degree < k (number of physical registers) onto a stack; when stuck, pick a spill candidate by cost heuristic (spill cost / degree ratio weighing use/def frequency against loop nesting depth). Briggs's refinement makes coloring **optimistic**: potential spills are still pushed and only actually spilled if, during the select phase, no color remains, since a high-degree node may still be colorable if its neighbors don't use all k colors. **Coalescing** merges move-related nodes to eliminate copies; **conservative (Briggs) coalescing** only merges nodes whose combined neighbor set has fewer than k high-degree neighbors, while **George/Appel iterated coalescing** interleaves simplify, coalesce, freeze, and spill steps to coalesce more aggressively without compromising colorability.

**Linear scan register allocation.** Computes live intervals (start/end points over a linearized instruction order) instead of a full interference graph, then allocates registers via a greedy sweep, assigning free registers and evicting/spilling the interval with the furthest next use when none are free. **Interval splitting** breaks a long live interval into pieces so parts can live in registers and parts can be spilled, reducing wasted spill code. Its lower setup cost (no graph construction) makes it the standard choice for JIT compilers under compile-time pressure (V8's early Crankshaft/pre-Turbofan allocator, early-tier LLVM `-O0`), trading some code quality for allocation speed. "Second-chance" binpacking variants allow previously spilled values to be reconsidered for registers later in the same scan.

**SSA-based register allocation (Hack, Grund, Goos).** Exploits the theorem that interference graphs of programs in strict SSA form are **chordal**, meaning they can be colored optimally in polynomial time without the heuristic simplify/spill iteration graph coloring needs for general graphs. The allocator performs coloring directly on the chordal graph, then handles the register-pressure-exceeded case by spilling before coloring (computing max pressure per program point and spilling to bring pressure under k), followed by live-range splitting at points where values cross high-pressure regions. This separates the spilling decision from the coloring decision cleanly, unlike Chaitin-Briggs where they're interleaved.

**PBQP-based allocation.** Formulates register assignment as Partitioned Boolean Quadratic Programming: each virtual register is a variable with a cost vector over candidate colors, and each interference/affinity edge contributes a cost matrix. PBQP solving (reduction rules for degree ≤2 nodes, heuristic branch-and-bound otherwise) naturally expresses irregular register constraints (overlapping register classes, odd/even register pairing, pre-colored operands for calling conventions) that graph coloring's simplify/select handles awkwardly. Used in LLVM's PBQP allocator for architectures with such irregularities (historically used for some embedded targets).

**Trade-offs.** Graph coloring with coalescing gives the best code quality for AOT compilation at higher compile time; linear scan trades quality for speed in JITs; SSA-based allocation offers clean separation of spilling and coloring with polynomial guarantees but requires maintaining strict SSA through the backend; PBQP handles architecture irregularity gracefully at higher per-function solve cost.

## 4. Inlining

**Cost-benefit heuristic inlining.** Both GCC and LLVM estimate a numeric "inline cost" from the callee's instruction count, call overhead saved, and benefits like constant-argument specialization, then compare against a threshold (adjusted by optimization level and context, e.g. hot call sites get a bonus). Explicit attributes (`always_inline`, `noinline`, `inline` hints) override the heuristic. Growth thresholds prevent unbounded code bloat from naive always-inline policies.

**Call graph SCC traversal order.** LLVM's Inliner pass processes the call graph bottom-up by strongly connected component (post-order on the SCC DAG), inlining leaf/callee functions before their callers so that a caller's cost estimate reflects the callee's *already-inlined-and-optimized* body, improving decision accuracy versus a naive top-down order which would estimate against un-simplified callees. Recursive SCCs (mutually recursive functions) are handled specially since there's no acyclic order within the cycle.

**Partial inlining / hot-cold splitting.** Rather than inlining an entire callee, only a hot subset of its control flow (e.g. a fast-path with few instructions) is inlined, while the cold remainder stays a real out-of-line call. Function splitting more generally separates rarely executed blocks (identified via profile data or heuristics like blocks after an `unlikely`-annotated branch) into a separate cold section, improving icache locality for hot code without that benefit being purely about inlining.

**Speculative devirtualization + guarded inlining.** For virtual/indirect calls, the compiler inserts a runtime type/class check guarding an inlined fast path for the historically-observed receiver type, falling back to the generic virtual call otherwise. JIT compilers combine this with runtime feedback: V8's inline caches record observed receiver shapes at a call site and promote monomorphic/polymorphic sites to guarded inlining; HotSpot uses Class Hierarchy Analysis (CHA) to prove a virtual call has only one possible target statically, permitting unconditional devirtualization, with deoptimization support if a new subclass is later loaded.

**Profile-guided inlining.** Uses PGO edge and block execution counts to prioritize inlining decisions toward call sites that are actually hot at runtime, instead of relying purely on static heuristics (callee size, static call frequency estimates), improving both precision of the cost model and avoiding wasted code growth from inlining cold call sites.

**Recursive inlining limits.** Direct or mutual recursion requires explicit depth/size budgets (e.g. a maximum inlining depth or total growth factor per top-level function) to avoid non-termination or exponential code blow-up; GCC/LLVM both cap recursive inlining depth separately from the general cost threshold.

## 5. Escape Analysis

**Connection-graph-based escape analysis (HotSpot style).** Builds a connection graph tracking points-to and deferred edges between object allocation sites, fields, and local variables, then classifies each allocation as **NoEscape** (never leaves the method or any inlined callee, enabling scalar replacement and allocation elision), **ArgEscape** (passed to a callee but not stored globally or returned, allowing stack allocation but not full elimination), or **GlobalEscape** (potentially visible outside the method, e.g. returned, stored to a static/heap field, or passed to an unanalyzed call), which forces heap allocation.

**Scalar Replacement of Aggregates (SROA) enabled by escape analysis.** Once an allocation is proven NoEscape, its fields can be replaced by independent SSA scalars (no longer a single heap object), eliminating the allocation entirely and letting downstream optimizations (constant propagation, dead code elimination) operate on the individual fields as ordinary values rather than through memory loads/stores.

**Lock elision via escape analysis.** If an object used as a lock monitor is proven thread-local (NoEscape, or escapes only to a known-non-concurrent context), HotSpot removes the actual monitor acquire/release (synchronization elimination / lock elision), since no other thread can ever observe or compete for that lock.

**Partial escape analysis (Graal).** Instead of a binary escapes/doesn't-escape classification per allocation, tracks escape state per control-flow path and allows an object to be virtual (scalar-replaced) along some paths and materialized (actually allocated) only at the specific merge point where it starts escaping, via **allocation merging**: if two branches produce differently-shaped virtual objects that merge, the compiler materializes a real object only at the merge, keeping the rest of each branch allocation-free.

**Context-sensitive (object-sensitive) interprocedural escape analysis.** Extends escape classification across call boundaries with context sensitivity (e.g. 1-object-sensitivity, distinguishing allocation sites by the receiver object of the enclosing call) so that the same method called with a locally-allocated object in one context and an externally-visible one in another gets different escape conclusions per context instead of one conservative merged answer.

**Go compiler's escape analysis.** Performs a whole-function (and limited interprocedural) analysis to decide stack vs heap placement for every allocation; anything that could outlive its declaring frame (returned by pointer, stored into a heap-reachable structure, or captured by an escaping closure) is forced to the heap ("moves to heap", visible via `-m` diagnostics), while everything else is stack-allocated with no GC involvement, directly reducing GC pressure.

## 6. Loop Vectorization

**Superword-Level Parallelism (SLP) vectorization (Larsen & Amarasinghe).** Identifies groups of **isomorphic** scalar statements (same opcode, compatible types) operating on adjacent memory or independent data within or across basic blocks, packs them into a single vector operation, and inserts pack/unpack glue where a vector value feeds or is fed by scalar code that wasn't vectorized. Unlike loop vectorization, SLP doesn't require a loop; it operates on straight-line code with repeated similar statements, as implemented in LLVM's SLPVectorizer.

**Loop-level (outer) vectorization.** The LLVM Loop Vectorizer selects a **vectorization factor (VF)** (how many loop iterations execute per vector instruction) and an **interleave/unroll factor** (how many VF-wide groups are unrolled together to hide latency and improve instruction-level parallelism), guided by a cost model comparing estimated vector-code cost against scalar-code cost for candidate VFs, factoring in target vector register width and available vector ISA extensions.

**Dependence testing for vectorization legality.** Loop-carried dependences are checked via tests such as the **GCD test** (checks whether an integer solution exists to the dependence equation via the greatest common divisor of coefficients, a necessary but not sufficient condition), **Banerjee's test** (bounds-based test checking whether the dependence equation has a solution within the loop's iteration bounds), and more precise exact methods like the **Omega test** (integer linear programming–based, exact but costlier). These produce **distance vectors** and **direction vectors** per loop nest level that determine whether a dependence is loop-carried and in which direction, which vectorization legality checks consume directly: a negative/unknown direction on a carried dependence generally blocks vectorization unless the dependence distance exceeds the vector width.

**Reduction and induction variable handling, and if-conversion.** Vectorizing a reduction loop (e.g. summation) requires recognizing the reduction pattern and transforming it into a vector accumulator plus a final horizontal reduction step, rather than treating the dependence as a blocking loop-carried hazard. Induction variables are similarly recognized and vectorized by computing a vector of per-lane offsets. Control flow inside the loop body (if/else) is handled by **if-conversion (predication)**: conditional stores/updates become predicated/masked vector operations instead of branches, since vector lanes can't diverge in SIMD execution.

**Vector masking / predicated execution.** Handles loop remainder iterations (when the trip count isn't a multiple of VF) and genuinely divergent per-lane control flow using hardware mask registers, as in AVX-512's `k`-mask registers or ARM SVE's predicate registers, letting the compiler emit a single masked vector instruction instead of a separate scalar remainder loop, improving code density and avoiding a costly fallback path.

**Strip mining.** Transforms the original loop into an outer loop iterating in chunks of size VF and an inner (fully unrolled) vector body operating on one VF-wide chunk, which is the structural precursor transformation that loop vectorizers apply before actually emitting vector instructions; it cleanly separates the "how many iterations per vector op" decision from the vector codegen itself and naturally produces the remainder loop that masking or a scalar tail then handles.

## 7. Instruction Scheduling

**List scheduling.** The baseline local (basic-block) scheduling algorithm: build a data-dependence graph (DDG) over the block's instructions (true/anti/output dependences plus resource constraints), compute a priority for each ready instruction (commonly critical-path length to the end of the block, i.e. highest-latency-first), and greedily pick the next instruction to issue from the ready list each cycle according to priority, respecting functional-unit and latency constraints. Variants differ in direction: **forward (ASAP-biased)** scheduling fills from block entry; **backward (ALAP-biased)** list scheduling works from the block's exit, which can produce different register-pressure profiles for the same block.

**Software pipelining / modulo scheduling.** Targets loop bodies on VLIW/DSP architectures by overlapping iterations: compute the **Minimum Initiation Interval (MII)** as the maximum of the resource-constrained MII (total resource usage per iteration divided by available units) and the recurrence-constrained MII (longest cyclic dependence chain's latency divided by its distance in iterations), then schedule operations into a repeating pattern with that initiation interval, generating a **prologue** (fills the pipeline), a steady-state **kernel** (the repeating overlapped body), and an **epilogue** (drains it). This exposes instruction-level parallelism across loop iterations that local scheduling within one iteration cannot.

**Trace scheduling (Fisher).** Extends scheduling beyond a single basic block by selecting a **trace**: a sequence of basic blocks along the most probable execution path, determined from static heuristics or profile data, then scheduling across the whole trace as if it were one block, hoisting and reordering instructions across block boundaries. Because execution can leave the trace at any branch, the algorithm inserts **compensation code** on off-trace edges to preserve correctness when an instruction's movement past a branch would otherwise change behavior for the non-predicted path.

**Region-based scheduling: superblocks and hyperblocks.** A **superblock** is a trace with side entrances removed (via tail duplication), giving it a single entry and possibly multiple exits, which simplifies compensation code since there's no need to handle code motion around unpredictable entry points. A **hyperblock** goes further, combining **if-conversion** (predicating short conditional regions into straight-line code using predicate registers) with superblock formation to merge multiple control-flow paths into one large schedulable region, maximizing exposed ILP for VLIW targets at the cost of executing some predicated-off work.

**Register-pressure-aware scheduling and phase ordering.** Maximizing ILP by reordering instructions for parallelism tends to lengthen live ranges and increase register pressure, which can force the register allocator to spill, erasing the scheduling gain. Pressure-sensitive heuristics bias the priority function to prefer instructions that shorten live ranges (e.g. prioritizing consumers of already-live values over producers of new long-lived values) when pressure is high. Because scheduling before allocation can create pressure that forces spills, while scheduling after allocation is constrained by the fixed register assignment and can't freely reorder across false dependences introduced by reuse, compilers either schedule twice (pre- and post-allocation passes) or use integrated heuristics that estimate pressure during a single pre-allocation schedule — this is the classic scheduling/register-allocation **phase-ordering problem**.

## 8. Loop Optimizations

**Loop-Invariant Code Motion (LICM).** Identifies computations whose operands are all loop-invariant (defined outside the loop or themselves invariant) and hoists them to the loop preheader. For memory operations, a load can only be hoisted if alias analysis proves no store in the loop may write the same location (and no intervening call has unknown side effects on it); such **speculative hoisting** also requires that the load is safe to execute unconditionally (won't trap) if the original was only conditionally executed, otherwise non-speculative hoisting applies only to loads provably executed on every iteration. The complementary **sinking** moves loop-invariant stores or late-used values out of the loop toward their actual uses when hoisting isn't legal but delaying is beneficial. In LLVM, LICM operates cleanly over **loop-closed SSA form (LCSSA)**, where every value used outside a loop gets a dedicated φ-node at the loop exit, which simplifies reasoning about what crosses the loop boundary.

**Loop unrolling and unroll-and-jam.** Full unrolling replicates the entire loop body for a statically known small trip count, eliminating branch overhead entirely. Partial unrolling replicates the body by a chosen unroll factor and adjusts the trip count/remainder handling, exposing more instructions per iteration to scheduling and vectorization (larger blocks give list scheduling and SLP more candidates) at the cost of code size and potentially higher register pressure. **Unroll-and-jam** unrolls an outer loop in a nest and then fuses (jams) the resulting copies of the inner loop back together, increasing reuse of inner-loop-invariant values across what were separate outer iterations, improving cache/register reuse in nested loops without full unrolling.

**Strength reduction and induction variable simplification.** Replaces expensive operations (e.g. multiplication by the loop index) with cheaper equivalents (addition) by recognizing **induction variables** — variables that change by a fixed amount each iteration — and representing derived expressions (like array address computations) as increments of a dedicated induction variable rather than recomputing them from the loop counter each time. **Linear function test replacement** goes further, rewriting the loop's exit test itself to use a strength-reduced induction variable instead of the original counter, when doing so lets the original counter be eliminated entirely as dead.

**Loop fusion and fission (distribution).** **Fusion** merges two adjacent loops with compatible iteration spaces into one, reducing loop overhead and improving data locality (if both touch the same array, the second loop's accesses may now hit cache from the first loop's traversal); legality requires that fusing doesn't violate any dependence that existed between the two original loops (no statement in the second loop may depend on a later iteration's computation from the first loop after fusion). **Fission/distribution** does the reverse, splitting one loop into several, each handling a subset of the original statements, which can be legal (and profitable) when a single loop mixes vectorizable and non-vectorizable statement groups, letting the vectorizable part become its own clean loop.

**Loop interchange.** Swaps the nesting order of two loops in a loop nest (e.g. row-major vs column-major traversal) to improve spatial locality for cache access patterns, typically to make the innermost loop stride through memory contiguously. Legality is determined from the dependence **direction vectors** for the nest: interchange is legal only if it doesn't turn a forward dependence into a backward one in the new nesting order (informally, if swapping wouldn't make the loop read data that, in program order, hasn't been computed yet, i.e. it preserves all dependence direction consistency).

**Loop tiling / blocking.** Splits a loop nest's iteration space into smaller tiles (blocks) sized to fit the working set within a given cache level, with an outer loop iterating over tiles and an inner loop iterating within a tile, trading a single large sweep over data (which thrashes cache) for repeated smaller sweeps that stay resident. Tile size selection must balance cache capacity against loop overhead from the added tiling loops, and tiling legality again rests on dependence analysis to ensure the chosen tile traversal order doesn't violate any cross-iteration dependence.

**Interaction with downstream passes.** LICM reduces redundant work before vectorization/scheduling even see the loop body; unrolling and fusion enlarge the scheduling region and the candidate set for SLP; interchange and tiling restructure memory access order specifically so the loop vectorizer's cost model (which assumes contiguous, well-strided access for best vector/memory throughput) finds a profitable vectorization; strength reduction removes address-computation overhead that would otherwise compete with vector lanes for functional units. Legality for nearly all loop-nest transformations (fusion, fission, interchange, tiling, unroll-and-jam) is governed by the same underlying dependence analysis infrastructure (distance/direction vectors, the tests described in Section 6) that also gates loop vectorization, so these passes are tightly coupled in practice rather than independent.

---

Answer: The brief above covers all eight areas with the required depth: SSA construction (Cytron's dominance-frontier algorithm, Braun et al.'s local-first incremental construction with block sealing, Sreedhar & Gao's DJ-graph IDF computation, plus SSA destruction/lost-copy and SSI form); alias analysis (Andersen's inclusion-based analysis, Steensgaard's unification-based analysis, type-based alias analysis/TBAA, flow/context-sensitivity, and MOD/REF summaries); register allocation (Chaitin-Briggs graph coloring with Briggs/George-Appel coalescing, linear scan with interval splitting, SSA-based chordal-graph allocation, and PBQP-based allocation); inlining (cost-benefit heuristic models, SCC-based bottom-up call graph traversal, partial inlining/hot-cold splitting, speculative devirtualization with CHA/inline caches, and PGO-guided inlining); escape analysis (HotSpot connection-graph classification, SROA-enabling scalar replacement, lock elision, Graal's partial escape analysis with allocation merging, and Go's stack/heap escape diagnostics); loop vectorization (SLP vectorization, LLVM's loop vectorizer with VF/interleave cost modeling, GCD/Banerjee/Omega dependence tests, reduction/induction recognition with if-conversion, masking/predication, and strip mining); instruction scheduling (list scheduling, software pipelining/modulo scheduling with MII computation, trace scheduling with compensation code, superblock/hyperblock region scheduling, and the scheduling/register-allocation phase-ordering problem); and loop optimizations (LICM with LCSSA, unrolling and unroll-and-jam, strength reduction with linear function test replacement, loop fusion/fission, loop interchange, and loop tiling), with explicit discussion throughout of legality conditions, profitability heuristics, and cross-pass interactions.

response.content:
# SECTION 1: SSA CONSTRUCTION

## 1.1 Cytron et al. Dominance-Frontier Algorithm

The classical algorithm from Cytron, Ferrante, Rosen, Wegman, and Zadeck (1991) constructs semi-pruned or minimal SSA via explicit dominator-tree analysis and iterated dominance frontiers (IDF).

**Dominator tree construction.** A node `d` dominates `n` if every path from entry to `n` passes through `d`. The immediate dominator `idom(n)` is the closest strict dominator, and the dominator tree is the tree formed by the `idom` relation. Production implementations use the Lengauer-Tarjan algorithm, achieving O(E log V) (near-linear in practice with path compression), rather than the naive iterative dataflow fixpoint (O(N^2) or worse on irreducible CFGs). Lengauer-Tarjan computes semidominators via DFS numbering and a union-find-like structure over a spanning forest, then derives `idom` from semidominators in a second pass.

**Dominance frontier.** `DF(n)` is the set of nodes `m` such that `n` dominates a predecessor of `m` but does not strictly dominate `m` itself — informally, the first points where control flow merges after branching at or below `n`. Cytron's local computation: for each node `n`, for each CFG successor `s`, if `idom(s) != n`, then `s ∈ DF(n)`; this seeds `DF_local(n)`. Then the frontier is propagated up the dominator tree: for each child `c` of `n` in the dominator tree, for each `w ∈ DF(c)`, if `n` does not strictly dominate `w`, add `w` to `DF(n)`. This bottom-up tree walk gives `DF` for all nodes in O(N·α) amortized under typical CFG shapes, though worst-case quadratic blowup is possible on pathological graphs with large frontiers.

**Iterated dominance frontier (IDF) and phi placement.** For a variable `v` with a set of definition blocks `Defs(v)`, the placement of phi-nodes requires the *iterated* dominance frontier: `DF+(S) = DF(S) ∪ DF(DF(S)) ∪ ...` until fixpoint. A phi-node for `v` is inserted at every block in `DF+(Defs(v))`. The standard worklist implementation processes blocks whose frontier hasn't yet been visited for this variable, using per-variable "has-already-been-processed" and "in-worklist" bitsets to avoid redundant insertion, giving the overall phi-insertion pass a complexity bounded by O(N) phi insertions per variable in practice (though theoretically the DF relation size can be superlinear).

**Renaming.** After phi placement, a second dominator-tree-driven pass renames each use to the reaching definition, maintaining a per-variable stack of SSA names pushed on definition and popped on scope-exit (post-order return from dominator-tree recursion), with phi operands filled in per predecessor edge based on current reaching names at the point control reaches that predecessor's exit.

**Correctness properties.** The Cytron algorithm produces **minimal SSA**: a phi-node is inserted at `w` for variable `v` iff `w` is in the iterated dominance frontier of `v`'s definitions — exactly the join points where two distinct definitions of `v` can reach. This is minimal in the sense of inserting no more phis than necessary for *some* definition set reaching a merge, but it is not automatically **pruned**: minimal SSA may still insert phi-nodes for variables that are not live past the merge point. **Pruned SSA** additionally requires liveness information to suppress phi-nodes for dead variables, typically computed via a prior liveness analysis and intersected with the IDF-based placement set.

**Complexity.** Dominator tree: near-linear via Lengauer-Tarjan (practically O(N log N) or better with simple variants on typical CFGs). DF computation: O(N^2) worst case but near-linear in practice. Renaming: O(N + V·D) where D relates to phi/use counts. Overall the classical pipeline is efficient for AOT optimizing compilers willing to pay preprocessing cost for precise, minimal results used repeatedly across many optimization passes.

## 1.2 Braun et al. Simple and Efficient Construction of SSA Form

Braun, Buchwald, Hack, Leißa, Mallon, and Zwinkau (2013) present a construction algorithm that avoids computing dominator trees or dominance frontiers up front, instead building SSA incrementally during a single forward pass over the CFG, suitable for incremental/JIT-style compilation where the CFG may be discovered on the fly.

**Local value numbering per block.** Within a basic block, variable definitions are tracked in a simple local map `currentDef[block][var]`. A read of `var` in `block` first checks this local map; if absent, the algorithm recurses to find the *global* value via `readVariableRecursive`, which consults predecessor blocks.

**Handling incomplete predecessors.** Because blocks may be processed before all their predecessors are known (e.g., forward branches, loop back-edges not yet constructed), the algorithm distinguishes between completed and incomplete blocks. For an incomplete block, a phi-node is optimistically inserted and marked as an *operandless placeholder*; its operands are filled in later once all predecessors are known, via `addPhiOperands`. This defers phi-completion rather than requiring the full CFG upfront, which is exactly the property needed for streaming/JIT front-ends (e.g., bytecode-to-IR translation processing one basic block at a time).

**Sealing blocks.** A block is "sealed" once all of its predecessors are known and processed. Only sealed blocks have their phi-node operand lists finalized. Reading a variable in an unsealed block inserts a placeholder phi and defers; sealing a block triggers `addPhiOperands` for all pending phis in that block, which recursively looks up the current definition of the variable along each predecessor edge via `readVariable`.

**Recursive lookup and the join rule.** `readVariableRecursive(var, block)`: if `block` has exactly one predecessor, recurse into that predecessor directly (no phi needed — this is the key local-optimization avoiding redundant phis on straight-line/single-predecessor chains). If multiple predecessors, insert a phi-node, record it as the block's current definition (to handle self-referential/cyclic lookups, e.g. loop headers, breaking infinite recursion), then populate operands by recursively reading the variable from each predecessor.

**Trivial phi removal (minimal/pruned SSA via local rewriting).** The naive construction can introduce redundant phis — e.g., a phi whose operands are all the same value, or all refer to itself plus one other value (common at loop headers for variables not actually modified in the loop). `tryRemoveTrivialPhi` detects such patterns: if all non-self operands of a phi are identical (or the phi only refers to itself), the phi is replaced by that single value and removed, with uses rewritten to point to the surviving value. This removal must be applied transitively, since removing one trivial phi can make a dependent phi trivial (classic in nested loop headers). This local phi-pruning gives SSA that is provably **minimal** under the same join-point definition as Cytron's IDF, without ever computing dominance frontiers explicitly — the paper proves the two algorithms produce equivalent (semantically isomorphic, phi-for-phi after pruning) minimal SSA for a given CFG.

**Why preferred in JIT compilers.** Cranelift and LLVM's `-O0`/fast-ISel-style paths favor Braun's construction because:
- No separate dominator-tree or dominance-frontier precomputation pass is required; everything happens in one traversal, reducing constant-factor compile time, critical for JIT warm-up latency.
- It naturally supports incremental/on-the-fly IR building as bytecode is decoded linearly, with loop back-edges resolved via the seal-later mechanism — exactly matching how JITs translate bytecode basic-block by basic-block.
- The trivial-phi-removal step gives "good enough" minimal SSA cheaply, avoiding the need for a full liveness-based pruning pass, which matters when compile time dominates the cost/benefit ratio (as in JIT tiers that will be replaced by a higher optimization tier anyway).

Classic Cytron remains favored in AOT optimizing compilers (e.g., GCC's tree-SSA, LLVM's `-O2`/`-O3` IR-construction-from-already-built-CFG scenarios where the whole function is available upfront) because the dominator tree and dominance frontiers, once computed, are reused extensively by *many* downstream passes (loop-invariant code motion needs dominator info; GVN/PRE needs dominance queries for safety of hoisting; SSA-aware dead code elimination uses dominance). Paying the precomputation cost once amortizes across the whole pass pipeline, and dominator trees give O(1) or O(log N) dominance queries thereafter (via DFS in/out numbering), which Braun's algorithm does not directly produce as a byproduct.

## 1.3 Sreedhar & Gao's DJ-Graph Algorithm

Sreedhar and Gao (1995) address the practical cost of iterated-dominance-frontier computation, which in Cytron's formulation can require materializing dominance-frontier sets that are themselves large (quadratic in pathological cases) even though the *final* set of phi insertion points is usually small.

**DJ-graph structure.** The DJ-graph overlays two edge kinds on the CFG's node set: **D-edges**, which are exactly the dominator-tree edges (`idom` edges), and **J-edges**, which are the original CFG join edges `(a, b)` where `a` does not dominate `b` (i.e., edges that cross or merge control flow rather than simply extending dominance). This structure captures exactly the information needed for dominance-frontier-like queries without materializing the frontier sets themselves.

**Key insight — level-bounded J-edges.** For a J-edge `(a,b)` in the DJ-graph, the algorithm shows that `b`'s level (depth in the dominator tree) is less than or equal to `a`'s level in well-structured cases, and the iterated-dominance-frontier computation can be reformulated as a traversal that walks *up* from J-edge targets through D-edges, bounded by level comparisons, rather than doing the explicit "DF of DF of DF..." fixpoint over materialized sets.

**Piggy-back/merge-set and DJ+ algorithm.** The refined version maintains, for each dominator-tree node, a *merge set* computed via a single bottom-up traversal of the dominator tree combined with J-edge lookups: when processing node `n`, examine all J-edges incident to nodes in `n`'s dominator subtree, and determine which ancestors in the dominator tree are "exposed" as join points. This avoids the pairwise set-union propagation of DF(c) into DF(n) that Cytron's algorithm performs explicitly. The algorithm achieves **O(E)** or near-linear time for computing all the information needed to place phi-nodes (matching the asymptotic bound of the dominator-tree construction itself), compared to Cytron's approach which is linear in well-behaved programs but can degrade due to materialized DF-set sizes.

**Practical trade-off.** The DJ-graph method is primarily valuable for very large functions or whole-program/interprocedural-scale IR construction (e.g., in some research AOT infrastructures) where dominance-frontier set sizes could become a real bottleneck. For typical function-sized CFGs in production compilers, Cytron's direct DF computation is simple to implement and fast enough in practice, so DJ-graph-based IDF is more of a theoretical/asymptotic improvement that sees adoption mainly in compilers emphasizing scalability guarantees rather than typical-case constant factors.

## 1.4 SSA Destruction and Out-of-SSA Translation

Converting back to a non-SSA (conventional) form for code generation requires eliminating phi-nodes while preserving program semantics — this is substantially harder than it looks because of **parallel copy semantics** at block boundaries.

**Phi semantics and parallel copies.** A phi-node `x = phi(x1 from B1, x2 from B2, ...)` executes conceptually as a simultaneous (parallel) assignment at the *start* of its block, sourced from the *end* of each respective predecessor. Naive translation inserts a copy `x = xi` at the end of predecessor `Bi`, but this is only correct if the copies inserted across multiple phi-nodes in the same block, and across predecessors, are treated as happening in parallel rather than sequentially.

**The lost-copy problem.** Arises when a value needed by a later phi operand is overwritten by an earlier-inserted copy for a different phi in the same critical edge/predecessor. Example: a block with two phis `x = phi(y, ...)` and `y = phi(x, ...)` coming from the same predecessor — naively inserting `x := y; y := x` sequentially loses the original value of `x` before it's used to set `y`. This is the classic **swap problem**: when phi operands in the same predecessor reference each other circularly (`x := y` and `y := x` simultaneously), sequential copy insertion corrupts the result unless a temporary is used or the copies are recognized as a permutation and implemented via a sequence of swaps/rotations through a temporary register.

**Standard solution — sequentializing parallel copies.** The accepted technique (following Briggs et al. and later refined, e.g. by Boissinot et al.) is to:
1. Insert phi-node-implied copies on edges (using **edge splitting** to insert a new empty block on critical edges — edges where the source has multiple successors and the target has multiple predecessors — so that copies for one successor don't affect code reaching other successors).
2. Treat all copies implied by phis within one predecessor-to-successor transition as one **parallel copy** instruction/set.
3. Sequentialize the parallel copy set via a dependency graph over copy destinations/sources: copies with no conflicting dependency can be ordered arbitrarily; cyclic dependencies (the swap case) are broken by introducing a temporary variable to hold one value while the cycle is unwound, or by using an explicit swap operation if the target ISA supports it.

**Coalescing.** After sequentialization, naive copy insertion produces many redundant move instructions. **Copy coalescing** merges SSA names connected by a copy into the same physical storage location when it's safe to do so — i.e., when their live ranges don't interfere (standard interference-graph-based coalescing as in Chaitin-style register allocation) and they are connected by a phi-induced or direct copy. **Aggressive coalescing** can merge more variables but risks increasing interference-graph degree and causing spills; **conservative coalescing** (e.g., Briggs-style or George/Appel iterated coalescing) only merges when safe under a degree bound, trading away some copy elimination for allocation quality. This phase is critical because the raw SSA-destruction output, if left uncoalesced, can double or triple the number of move instructions compared to hand-written non-SSA code.

**Dominance property of correct SSA (useful invariant).** Correctly constructed SSA guarantees each use is dominated by its (unique) definition; this invariant is exploited during destruction to validate copy placement and during register allocation (e.g., SSA-based "linear scan" or "live range splitting" register allocators rely directly on the dominance property to simplify live-range computation, since live ranges in SSA form a tree-structured dominance relationship rather than arbitrary overlapping ranges).

## 1.5 Static Single Information (SSI) Form

SSI form (Ananian 1999; further developed by Singer) extends SSA by also giving each *use* site a unique name where control-flow splits downstream of a definition, achieved via **sigma-nodes** (or "pi-nodes" in some literatures) placed at branch points, symmetric to phi-nodes at merge points.

**Mechanism.** Where a phi-node merges multiple incoming definitions at a join point, a sigma-node splits a single value into multiple renamed copies at a branch point, one per outgoing edge, so that information specific to a branch outcome (e.g., "`x` is non-null in the true branch of `if (x != null)`," or range/predicate refinement from a comparison) can be attached to the branch-specific renamed copy without affecting uses on other paths.

**Use cases.** SSI is primarily valuable for analyses needing path-sensitive refinement without full path-sensitive analysis cost: null-check elimination, range propagation/refinement after comparisons, and sparse conditional constant propagation variants that want per-branch refined facts. It's also used to simplify some dataflow formulations (e.g., certain def-use-based sparse analyses become uniformly forward or uniformly backward sparse problems in SSI, whereas in plain SSA some analyses need extra bookkeeping at branches).

**Trade-offs.** SSI increases IR size (more renaming operations, more "virtual" nodes that are often no-ops at the machine level and must be coalesced away during lowering, exactly analogous to phi-node destruction). It is rarely used as the primary IR for general-purpose optimizing compilers (LLVM IR, e.g., is plain SSA, not SSI) but appears in specialized middle-end passes or research compilers focused on predicate/range-sensitive optimization, where the construction cost is justified by the specific analysis it enables.

# SECTION 2: ALIAS ANALYSIS

## 2.1 Andersen's Analysis — Inclusion-Based Points-To Analysis

Andersen's analysis (1994) computes, for each pointer-typed variable, a **points-to set** approximating the set of memory locations (abstract objects) it may point to, using **subset (inclusion) constraints**.

**Constraint generation.** For each statement, generate a constraint over points-to sets:
- `p = &a` → `a ∈ pts(p)` (base constraint).
- `p = q` → `pts(q) ⊆ pts(p)` (copy/subset constraint).
- `p = *q` → for all `a ∈ pts(q)`, `pts(a) ⊆ pts(p)` (load, conditional inclusion).
- `*p = q` → for all `a ∈ pts(p)`, `pts(q) ⊆ pts(a)` (store, conditional inclusion).

**Resolution.** These constraints form a graph where nodes are abstract variables/objects and edges represent subset relations; solving is iterative constraint propagation (worklist-based) until a fixpoint, since the conditional (load/store) constraints only activate once the relevant points-to sets are nonempty, meaning new subset edges can appear dynamically as `pts()` sets grow (this dynamic edge addition is exactly why it's "inclusion-based" rather than simple unification).

**Complexity.** Andersen's analysis is **cubic** in the size of the program in the worst case — O(n^3) — because points-to set sizes can be O(n), the constraint graph has O(n) nodes, and propagating each element through each edge can require O(n) rounds, giving O(n^3) total work in the naive formulation. Practical implementations (e.g., using BDs as in `bddbddb`, or offline variable substitution / cycle-elimination preprocessing as in Hardekopf & Lin's work) achieve large practical speedups, but the underlying worst-case complexity class remains cubic (and has been shown to be close to a tight lower bound for the general inclusion-constraint problem).

**Precision.** Andersen's is **flow-insensitive** (one points-to set per variable for the whole program, not per program point) but is context-insensitive by default; it is considerably more precise than Steensgaard's because subset constraints preserve directionality — `pts(q) ⊆ pts(p)` does not force `pts(p) ⊆ pts(q)`, so a variable assigned-from doesn't get polluted with everything the assigned-to variable points to elsewhere, unlike unification.

## 2.2 Steensgaard's Analysis — Unification-Based

Steensgaard's analysis (1996) sacrifices precision for speed by using **unification (equality) constraints** instead of subset constraints, modeled directly on efficient union-find.

**Constraint model.** Each pointer variable is mapped to a node in a union-find structure representing an equivalence class with an associated "points-to" edge to another equivalence class. Assignment `p = q` *unifies* the points-to targets of `p` and `q` — instead of adding a one-directional subset edge, both variables' pointees are merged into a single equivalence class. This means if `p` can point to `a` and `q` can point to `b`, after `p = q`, both `p` and `q` are considered to point to the unified `{a, b}` class, and crucially this imprecision propagates transitively to every other variable connected to `p` or `q`, even those assigned before the unifying statement was processed.

**Complexity.** Near-linear — O(n log n) or practically O(n) with union-find path compression and union-by-rank — because each unification operation is amortized near-constant time and the number of unify operations is bounded by the program size, with no iterative fixpoint re-propagation of growing per-node sets as in Andersen's.

**Precision trade-off.** The loss of precision from unification can be severe: merging two variables' points-to targets because they were ever assigned to each other means all future and past aliasing relationships of either variable bleed into the other, producing much larger (less precise) effective points-to sets, especially around variables that are reassigned many times (e.g., loop induction-like pointer variables or generic container access patterns) — the classic example is that unifying through a single generic `malloc`-wrapper call can cause huge numbers of unrelated allocation sites to collapse into one equivalence class.

**Use case.** Steensgaard's analysis is preferred when scalability to very large codebases (whole-program C/C++ analysis in some static analysis tools, or fast "good enough" alias info in some less optimization-aggressive compiler passes) matters more than optimization-grade precision; Andersen's is preferred when the extra precision materially improves downstream optimization opportunities (e.g., enabling more redundant loads to be eliminated or more loop-invariant code motion) and compile-time budget allows.

## 2.3 Type-Based Alias Analysis (TBAA)

TBAA infers non-aliasing relationships from the **static type system**, relying on language-level aliasing rules rather than points-to computation.

**Strict aliasing in C/C++.** The C/C++ standards specify that an object may only be accessed through an lvalue of a compatible type (its declared type, a `char`-family type, or a few other exceptions) — accessing an `int` through a `float*` is undefined behavior absent an explicit union or `memcpy`. Compilers exploit this: two memory accesses through pointers of incompatible, non-char types are assumed **not to alias**, without needing any points-to computation.

**LLVM's TBAA metadata.** LLVM encodes a type hierarchy as metadata (`!tbaa` attached to load/store instructions), structured as a tree with scalar type nodes and "struct path" nodes describing field offsets within aggregates; two accesses are assumed non-aliasing if their TBAA metadata paths are determined incompatible per the encoded tree, following rules close to C/C++ strict-aliasing but generalized to also encode struct-field-level distinctions (so that accesses to two different fields of the same struct, both typed `int`, can still be disambiguated via path-sensitive metadata rather than just base scalar type). This gives a lightweight, essentially free (metadata lookup, no fixpoint computation) alias query usable directly during instruction selection or mid-level optimization.

**Trade-offs.** TBAA is unsound in the presence of type-punning via unions, reinterpret-casts, or code compiled with `-fno-strict-aliasing`; compilers must respect the opt-out flag and frontends must correctly emit metadata only where strict-aliasing guarantees legitimately hold (a frequent source of real-world miscompilation bugs when frontends mis-tag unions or when code violates strict aliasing but was written assuming GCC/Clang wouldn't optimize based on types). Its benefit is near-zero runtime analysis cost and good precision specifically for disambiguating accesses of visibly different static types, which is common and valuable for vectorization (proving a float array write can't alias an unrelated struct pointer load, permitting the load to be hoisted above the store) and scalar redundancy elimination.

## 2.4 Flow-Sensitivity, Context-Sensitivity

**Flow-insensitive analysis** (as in classic Andersen's/Steensgaard's described above) computes one points-to set per variable valid for the entire program, ignoring program-point-specific kill/strong-update effects — a store `*p = &b` is treated as *adding* `b` to `pts(target-of-p)` rather than replacing it, since the analysis has no notion of "before" and "after" at that program point. This is sound (over-approximate) but imprecise, since it can't model that a pointer's target changes over time.

**Flow-sensitive analysis** computes points-to information per program point, supporting **strong updates** (replacing, not just adding to, a location's points-to set when a must-alias single-target pointer is stored through) when the analysis can prove a write target is unique. This requires computing in/out points-to sets at every CFG node analogous to classical dataflow analysis, with correspondingly higher cost — typically much more expensive than flow-insensitive variants (often requiring points-to-set-sized dataflow facts propagated per basic block, rather than one global map), limiting it to smaller scopes (per-function, or whole-program only with aggressive summarization) in practice.

**Context-sensitivity.** A context-insensitive interprocedural analysis merges points-to information across all call sites of a function, which can cause spurious aliasing when a function is called with genuinely different, non-aliasing argument pointers from different sites. Context-sensitive analysis distinguishes different calling contexts:
- **k-CFA (k-th order Control Flow Analysis)**, originating in Shivers' work on Scheme analysis, distinguishes contexts by the last `k` call sites on the call stack (approximated), giving increasingly precise but exponentially more expensive analysis as `k` grows; `k=0` degenerates to context-insensitive.
- **Call-string approach** (classical interprocedural dataflow, Sharir & Pnueli) tracks explicit call-site strings as context identifiers, truncated to bounded length for tractability, essentially a concretization of the same idea used in IFDS/IDE frameworks for precise, demand-driven interprocedural analysis.
- **Summary-based / functional approach** as an alternative to call-strings: compute a function summary (a transfer function from input alias/points-to state to output state) once per function and instantiate it at each call site, avoiding explicit context enumeration — this scales better for highly-called utility functions (e.g. allocators, generic container accessors) at some precision cost relative to true context-sensitivity.

The trade-off throughout is precision vs. scalability: context- and flow-sensitive analysis give far fewer false "may-alias" results (enabling more aggressive optimization) but can blow up super-linearly on real codebases, so production compilers typically use flow-insensitive, context-insensitive (or only mildly context-sensitive, e.g. one level of call-site cloning for small/hot functions) analysis as the default, reserving flow/context-sensitive variants for specialized tools (bug-finding static analyzers, security-focused taint analysis) willing to pay more for precision.

## 2.5 May-Alias vs Must-Alias, Alias Sets, MOD/REF Summaries

**May-alias vs must-alias.** A **may-alias** result means the analysis cannot prove two references are disjoint — they must be conservatively treated as possibly referring to the same memory, blocking reordering/elimination unless otherwise justified. A **must-alias** result is a positive proof that two references *always* refer to the same location, which is the stronger and rarer fact needed to justify **strong updates**, value forwarding without a branch on possible non-aliasing, or safely eliminating one of two redundant loads/stores. Most practical alias analyses are must-alias-weak and may-alias-focused, since must-alias requires much stronger reasoning (e.g., exact pointer arithmetic equality, or flow-sensitive strong-update tracking); shape analysis (see below) is one of the few techniques that routinely derives must-alias facts for structured heap data.

**Shape analysis.** Shape analysis (e.g., based on Three-Valued-Logic / TVL frameworks, Sagiv-Reps-Wilhelm) goes beyond points-to sets to characterize the *shape* of heap-allocated data structures (e.g., "this pointer always refers to an acyclic singly-linked list node not shared with any other live pointer"), enabling strong must-not-alias guarantees (e.g., proving two traversal pointers into disjoint list segments never alias) that plain points-to analysis cannot establish. This is substantially more expensive (abstract interpretation over 3-valued logical structures, often exponential in structure complexity) and mostly appears in verification tools or highly specialized compiler passes rather than general-purpose production optimizers, due to cost.

**Alias sets.** Many compiler IRs group memory locations into **alias sets** (or "alias classes") such that any two accesses to different alias sets are guaranteed non-aliasing, and accesses within the same set must be conservatively treated as potentially aliasing. This is a coarser, more implementation-convenient encoding of points-to/TBAA information — e.g., LLVM's older `AliasSetTracker` groups memory operations for loop-invariant code motion and dead-store elimination purposes, partitioning all memory references in a region into a small number of disjoint sets for fast "does this access conflict with that set" queries rather than doing full pairwise points-to-based queries.

**MOD/REF (modify/reference) summaries.** For interprocedural optimization, rather than exposing full points-to information at call sites, compilers compute per-function **MOD** (may-modify) and **REF** (may-reference/read) summaries: the set of abstract memory locations (or alias classes) a called function might write to or read from, respectively. These summaries let call sites treat a call as a black-box side-effecting operation with known conflict surface rather than requiring full interprocedural points-to resolution at every call. MOD/REF info feeds directly into:
- **GVN (global value numbering):** a load can be proven redundant with an earlier load of the same address only if no intervening MOD-summary-flagged call or store could have modified that address; MOD summaries let GVN safely value-number loads across call boundaries when the callee's MOD set doesn't overlap the loaded location's alias class.
- **LICM (loop-invariant code motion):** hoisting a load out of a loop, or sinking/eliminating a store, requires proving no store/call inside the loop body MODs the relevant address; alias-set/MOD-based summaries let LICM do this check in O(1) per candidate instruction against a precomputed per-loop "modified set" rather than re-querying full alias analysis per pair of instructions.
- **Vectorization:** proving that different loop iterations' memory accesses don't alias (no loop-carried dependence through aliasing pointers) is a prerequisite for safe vectorization; this typically combines alias analysis (to separate provably-disjoint base objects) with dependence analysis (to reason about access patterns/strides within a single base object), and REF/MOD summaries for any calls inside the loop body (e.g., calls to `pow`, library functions) determine whether the loop can be vectorized at all without inlining or specialized intrinsic recognition.

**Precision/scalability summary.** The overall design space is a lattice from cheap-and-imprecise (TBAA, unification-based Steensgaard, flow-insensitive alias sets) to expensive-and-precise (flow-sensitive context-sensitive Andersen's variants, shape analysis), and production compilers typically layer multiple techniques — e.g., LLVM uses TBAA as a fast, nearly-free first check, falls back to a flow-insensitive `BasicAA` (structural/offset reasoning plus limited points-to-like reasoning for `alloca`/globals), and composes results via an alias-analysis aggregation interface (`AAResults`) so that different downstream passes query whichever combination gives sufficient precision at acceptable cost for that specific optimization.
